title: Standard error vs standard deviation
reading_md:
**What it is.** The standard deviation (SD) describes the spread of single values: how much one order differs from another. The standard error (SE) describes the uncertainty of an estimate, such as a mean or a share: how much it would move from one sample to the next. The SE shrinks as the sample grows. The SD does not, because it is a property of the customers. The SE, not the SD, goes into a confidence interval.

**How to work it out.**

SE of a mean = s / √n

SE of a proportion = √(p × (1 - p) / n)

Worked example. Order values have an SD of €30 over n = 900 orders, with a mean of €60.

- √900 = 30.
- SE = 30 / 30 = €1.00 (2 decimals).
- 95% interval = 60 ± 1.96 × 1 = €58.04 to €61.96.

**In the interview.** "You collect 4 times more data. What happens to the SE, and to the SD?" A model answer: "The SE halves, because it divides by the square root of n, and √4 = 2. The SD stays roughly the same: more data does not make customers less varied."

**Common mistakes.**

- Using the SD instead of the SE in a confidence interval, which makes the interval far too wide.
- Believing more data reduces customer variability.
- Forgetting the square root: dividing by n instead of √n.
